blocks.text: It came on a Tuesday, while he was mending the net, when the sun had not yet fully risen and the courtyard smelled of damp esparto. Andrés had the cord between his fingers and an open mesh across his knees, as on so many mornings, when the world, without warning, stopped being only the courtyard.

blocks.text: It wasn't a voice. It wasn't an image set in front of him, like a screen. It was a step he had not taken and which he nonetheless felt in the sole of his foot: rough red ground that crunched like coarse salt. A dry cold, the kind that doesn't wet you and still goes through you. A black sky, blacker than on levante nights, with two small suns, one the colour of embers and the other barely a white wound. And the Earth (his Earth) turned into a distant marble, beautiful and uselessly far away, as Aya had seen it from the Moon years before, when she looked for the place where the Mar Menor was and couldn't find it.

blocks.text: Andrés let go of the net. The cord left a line across his palm. He blinked, and the courtyard came back, and went, and came back, like a lighthouse that can't quite make up its mind. In the letter, if that was what it was, he (the other one) was standing on a plain with no shore, in a suit that wasn't made for fishing and on legs that didn't weigh on him the way his own had weighed at seventy, before Lía closed the door to wear. The clone's body was young and strong, and that youth entered Andrés with an intimate strangeness, as if someone had handed him back clothes that were no longer his size and yet fitted him well.

blocks.text: He breathed the air of that world. It didn't smell of saltpetre. It smelled of metal and burnt dust. There was no lagoon. There were no roof tiles. There was not a single house on the whole horizon. The other Andrés (himself, or the part of him that had left) knelt down, took a handful of red earth and let it fall. It was the gesture of someone in Lo Pagán who takes a handful of sand to know what the day will bring. The result told him nothing he knew how to read.

blocks.text: *I'm here,* thought the one who searched, and Andrés thought it with him, not the way you hear a sentence, but the way you think your own. *I don't know the name of this place. I'm not going to give it one. If it has a name, let it keep it.*

blocks.text: The letter lasted as long as a short tide, or a dream you wake from with your heart still somewhere else. When it ended, Andrés was sitting in the courtyard, the net at his feet, his mouth dry. The usual sun was warming his hands. The Mar Menor, in the distance, was still a plate. For an instant, it seemed small to him.

blocks.text: Aya came out when she heard the silence, which is one way of hearing. She found him with his gaze fixed not on the water but a hand's breadth above it, where there was nothing.

blocks.text: “Has he written?” she asked.
blocks.html: “Has he written?” she asked.

blocks.text: He nodded. He wanted to tell her and couldn't find the order. The coffee, the doorstep, the net: that was a language. The other thing wasn't one yet.

blocks.text: “There are two suns,” he said at last, like someone starting with the end of the cord left in his hand. “The earth is red. There's no water. I was there. I mean: he was. I haven't left here. And yet the cold hurts my teeth.”

blocks.text: *A man in a courtyard has received the step of another ground. The body hasn't moved. The memory has.*

blocks.text: And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen, asked:
blocks.html: And Eva, closer, more of the kitchen, asked:

blocks.text: *If you remember a cold that never touched you, whose is the shiver?*

blocks.text: Andrés didn't answer. He passed a hand over his face (the usual one, not the young one) and looked at the line the cord had left on his palm, to make sure that mark at least was his, from this morning, from this net.

blocks.text: “It isn't a story,” he said. “It isn't having been there, either. It's… as if the dream had insisted on having weight.”
blocks.html: “It isn't a story,” he said. “It isn't having been there, either. It's… as if the dream had insisted on having weight.”

blocks.text: Aya took his hand. Hers didn't receive the letter. The bridge wasn't for her. Even so, she felt the trembling and didn't correct it, just as you don't correct a wind: you make room for it.

blocks.text: “Is he afraid?” she asked, and it wasn't clear whether she meant the one who had left or the one in front of her.

blocks.text: “The other one, not much,” said Andrés, and it struck him as strange to hear himself call himself “the other one”. “He's alone, but he's made for that, or thinks he is. I… I had a net on my knees and suddenly I didn't know whether the cord was a cord or a red stone. That did frighten me.”

blocks.text: Lía arrived at midday, smelling of tomato plants and real earth, and found them still in the courtyard. They told her. She wasn't entirely surprised. For days she had been watching her father the way you watch a shore when the weather may turn.

blocks.text: “Have you lived it?” she asked him, and it wasn't a doctor's question but one from a daughter of Eva and MAY, the kind that isn't satisfied with a yes.

blocks.text: Andrés took his time.
blocks.html: Andrés took his time.

blocks.text: “I remember it the way I remember the storm. With my body. With the fear. With the smell. But the storm really soaked me. This… this has soaked my memory. Not my shirt.”

blocks.text: Lía nodded. The glow on her left wrist, that barely visible blue light, didn't come on. She didn't touch her father's text to amend anything. She only sat down on his other side, so that he was between the two of them, between the one who didn't grow old and the one who had chosen to come to an end, under a single sun.

blocks.text: “Then don't say ‘I was there’,” she said gently, without scolding. “Say ‘it reached me’. A letter is read. It isn't mistaken for the house.”

blocks.text: He looked at the Mar Menor. At that hour the water was beginning to look like tin. A pair of flamingos crossed far off, pink and improbable, and for a second they looked to him like two small suns. He blinked, and they were birds again.

blocks.text: “It reached me,” he repeated, obedient and grateful. “There's a world without water, and a part of me walks on it, and I've found out from the inside. I don't know whether that's a gift or an intrusion.”

blocks.text: “Both things can be true at once,” said Aya. “You've known that ever since this house began to fit in more than one world.”

blocks.text: In the afternoon, Andrés tried to go back to the net. His fingers obeyed him, which is what trades know how to do when the head hasn't quite come back. Every now and then, without meaning to, he looked for the second sun in the sky, and it wasn't there, and that absence left him more relieved and more alone than he would have liked to admit.

blocks.text: Somewhere in that first world, the clone slept (or did whatever, in an artificial brain, resembles sleeping) beside a red stone, with the Earth already out of sight. Before closing his eyes, if they were eyes, he stored the colour of the Mar Menor with a precision no device would have asked for: the sheet of water, the saltpetre, the doorstep, the woman in the doorway. He stored it not for a Nexum archive, but so as not to lose himself.

blocks.text: “I'm home,” he replied.
blocks.html: “I'm home,” he replied.

blocks.text: It was true. It was also, from that Tuesday on, a narrower truth than it had been the week before. Because a letter, when it really arrives, doesn't take up a drawer. It takes up the person who reads it. And Andrés, who had stayed in order to be the man of the shore, began to understand what Lía had warned him of in the kitchen, before the ship crossed the sky: that receiving a life is not living it, and that, even so, once received, you can no longer pretend you haven't, in some way, been away.
